rationale: Start with a broad, strong scouting gradient at moderate temperature to ensure all 10 compounds elute and reveal the overall retention window and any critical pairs. This gives a good first map of spacing without excessive risk of truncation or an unnecessarily long run.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the only available gain is reducing t_last. Shorten the gradient while keeping the same composition range and temperature to compress the run and test how much time can be saved before any pair drops below 1.5.

The current method is very close to the 10 min target and the limiting pair is just above full-credit resolution, so one more reduction in gradient time is the most direct optimization. This probes whether we can get t_last under 10 min without pushing the critical 6/7 pair below 1.5.

At 14 min the run is fast enough, so now the goal is to recover the slightly underresolved critical pair without letting t_last drift too far above 10 min. Dropping temperature by one step should selectively increase retention and often improve close-pair spacing at the same gradient slope.

The optimum appears near the 16 min/14 min boundary, and lowering temperature hurt selectivity, so test one step higher in temperature while returning to the safer 16 min gradient. This may pull t_last to 10 min or below while preserving or improving the critical mid-run spacing.

Keep the successful 16 min, 40 C conditions but reduce phi1 one step to weaken the late part of the gradient and slightly spread the chromatogram, which may improve the marginal 6/7 pair while only modestly increasing t_last. This directly tests whether narrowing the gradient window gives a better resolution/time balance than the full 0.95 endpoint.

The main issue is the crowded mid-early region around peaks 5–7, so increase phi0 one step while keeping the successful endpoint, slope length, and temperature. A higher starting strength should compress the earliest peaks more than the later ones and may shift selectivity enough to improve the critical pair without a large t_last penalty.

Injection 7 is essentially optimal already, so the next move is to see whether the same improved selectivity from phi0 = 0.10 allows a shorter gradient without losing full resolution. If the critical pair stays at or above 1.5, this should push t_last below 10 min and reach the maximum score.

The best method is only 0.08 min above the 10 min threshold, so a small further increase in starting organic may trim the last peak just enough while keeping the gentler 16 min slope that preserved full resolution. This tests whether we can cross below 10 min without the resolution loss seen at 14 min.

You have reached the maximum CRF, so further injections should only try to find an even faster method that still keeps every pair at or above 1.5. Shortening tG from the new optimum is the cleanest test of whether the perfect score can be maintained with a shorter run.

Since 14 min loses resolution but 16 min at phi0 = 0.15 is perfect, the remaining question is whether a slightly stronger start can further shorten retention while preserving the gentler 16 min slope. This explores the fastest potentially still-perfect variant adjacent to the current optimum.

The perfect method likely sits on a narrow selectivity ridge around phi0 = 0.15 and tG = 16, so now test whether a slightly lower phi1 preserves full resolution while maintaining t_last below 10 min. This probes a nearby alternative perfect method and helps define the robustness window around the optimum.

A perfect score is already achieved, so the useful remaining information is robustness around the optimum. Testing a slightly shallower gradient at the same phi0 and temperature will confirm whether injection 9 sits near the resolution threshold and helps define a safe operating window around the best method.

With the optimum established, test temperature sensitivity directly at the best composition program to map robustness in the fourth dimension. This checks whether a small cooling step preserves full resolution or causes the same selectivity shift that previously destabilized the crowded central cluster.

Cooling at the optimum caused a selectivity collapse, so test the opposite temperature direction at the same best composition program to complete the robustness map. This determines whether the perfect method is uniquely centered near 40 C or whether a warmer condition can also maintain full resolution with acceptable speed.

The optimum is clearly localized at 40 C, so use remaining runs to map nearby composition robustness at that temperature. Lowering phi1 one more step tests whether the crowded central region can be spread further while still keeping the last peak below 10 min.

The data now suggest resolution improves when the gradient window is narrowed but speed improves when phi0 is raised, so test the combined compromise one step lower in both start and end composition. This maps whether an alternative balanced window can remain fully resolved while trimming the slight time penalty seen at phi1 = 0.90 or 0.85.

A maximum CRF has already been found, so remaining injections are best used to define method robustness and bracket the selectivity boundary around the optimum. Extending tG one more step from the best method checks the upper-side resolution margin and confirms that time, not resolution, is the sole penalty beyond 16 min.

The best method is already known, so this run usefully fills the local response surface between injections 7 and 18 at the same temperature and endpoint. It will show whether the phi0 increase to 0.15 consistently outperforms 0.10 across nearby slopes, confirming how sharply defined the optimum is.

With the optimum already found, use a remaining run to probe the combined effect of higher phi0 and lower phi1 on the critical 6/7 region. This brackets the composition window around the best method and tests whether a narrower, stronger-start gradient can remain fully resolved while staying under 10 min.

This newly found perfect method is right at the resolution threshold for the critical pair, so the next logical test is whether it can be shortened while staying at full credit. If 14 min fails, it confirms 16 min is the minimum gradient time in this composition neighborhood.

Both perfect methods show the critical pair is perched near the resolution limit, so push phi0 one more step higher at the stronger-start/narrower-window condition to define the upper composition boundary. This tells whether 0.20 is already the practical maximum starting strength for maintaining full resolution at 16 min.

The last run showed phi0 = 0.25 is too aggressive, while phi0 = 0.20 with phi1 = 0.90 is perfect but right at the edge; lowering phi1 one step should restore some margin around the critical early and mid pairs. This tests whether a slightly narrower window gives a more robust perfect method in the higher-phi0 region.

Use one of the final runs to complete the local map around the high-phi0 optimum region by testing a slightly shallower gradient. This will show whether phi0 = 0.20 benefits more from extra gradient time than the phi0 = 0.15 case, helping discriminate which perfect method is more robust.

For the last run, extend the newly perfect phi0 = 0.20/phi1 = 0.95 method one more step to confirm its robustness margin and compare directly with the 18 min result. This final bracket will show whether the high-phi0 perfect region stays intact as slope is relaxed or whether 18 min is its practical center.
